SDG&E Report on Public Safety Power Shutoff Event: January 14–16, 2021 
2 
This report covers the Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) protocols implemented in SDG&E’s 
service territory from January 14 through January 16, 2021.  As discussed below, while SDG&E 
initiated  its  PSPS  protocols,  including  customer  notifications,  SDG&E  did  not  de-energize 
customers for public safety in this time period. 
SDG&E submits this report to the Director of Safety 
and Enforcement Division (SED) and the service lists for Rulemaking (R.) 18-12-005 and R.18-
10-007.  This report includes the information required by Decision (D.) 12-04-024, Section II.A 
of CPUC Resolution ESRB-8, D.19-05-042, and D.20-05-051. 
 
The analysis and data provided in this report are based on the most current information available 
at the time and are subject to modification resulting from additional analyses and assessments 
completed following submission of the report. 
 
1. An  explanation  of  SDG&E’s  decision  to  de-energize,  including  an  explanation  of 
alternatives considered; mitigation measures used to decrease the risk of utility-caused 
wildfires in de-energized areas; a thorough and detailed description of the quantitative 
and qualitative factors SDG&E considered in calling, sustaining or curtailing the PSPS 
event,  including  information  regarding  why  PSPS  was  a  last  resort  option; and the 
specific conditions SDG&E determined must be present for the de-energization event to 
be concluded. 
Response: 
Explanation of the Decision to De-Energize  
The decision to initiate PSPS protocols was made at SDG&E’s Emergency Operations 
Center (EOC), which was staffed in a remote environment by a cross-functional team of 
electric operations, safety, meteorology, engineering, customer service, external affairs, 
communications, and other personnel, as well as a designated Utility Incident Commander 
(UIC) for the event. SDG&E implemented PSPS protocols to provide coordinated response; 
ensure there was informed decision-making; coordinate as-needed logistic support; and 
manage notifications to all affected stakeholders, including customers, state agencies, local 
jurisdictions, tribal governments, elected representatives, and public safety partners. 
SDG&E’s EOC was activated in a monitoring mode on January 13 at 1530 in response to 
weather forecasts indicating Santa Ana conditions, including strong winds and low humidity, 
were possible in portions of SDG&E’s service area.  Based on advanced forecasts, SDG&E 
anticipated the most severe winds and critical fire weather in areas of Orange County.  
SDG&E weighs many inputs when making the decision to de-energize portions of its system, 
and leverages refined situational awareness data and input from its subject matter experts 
when considering the need for PSPS, though experience with the program has indicated it is 
not appropriate to use a prescriptive technique to determine when to use PSPS, as wildfire 
conditions are dynamic and not every situation is the same.  When making the decision to de-
energize, SDG&E considers the following factors: 
• Weather conditions: SDG&E’s Fire Potential Index (FPI) ratings, Red Flag Warnings 
(RFW) issued by the National Weather Service (NWS), and the Santa Ana Wildfire 
Threat Index (SAWTI);

• Vegetation conditions and SDG&E’s Vegetation Risk Index; 
• Field observations and flying/falling debris; 
• Information from first responders; 
• Meteorological data, including 10-years of historical information from weather 
stations and 99th and 95th percentile winds; 
• Expected duration of conditions; 
• Location of any existing fires; 
• Wildfire activity in other parts of the state affecting resource availability; 
• Information on temporary construction. 
SDG&E has not developed a specific PSPS algorithm that lists, quantifies, and calculates the 
weight of each factor that is incorporated into a PSPS.  SDG&E has developed and published 
information regarding the factors and weights that go into the determination of the fire 
environment severity which is included in the FPI and SAWTI sections of SDG&E’s 2020 
Wildfire Mitigation Plan (WMP).1 
In addition to local weather conditions, SDG&E closely monitored and considered wildfire 
activity throughout the region and the availability of fire suppression resources to the area. 
After monitoring and considering weather conditions, de-energizations for public safety were 
not implemented during this event. The central considerations in determining if PSPS were 
warranted are detailed below. 
Weather Forecasts and Conditions 
Summary: The NWS issued a RFW for Inland Orange County (Zone 554) effective 
January 14 at 1600 until January 16 at 1600 for widespread gusty winds accompanied by 
hot and dry conditions. 
Weather Forecasts: SDG&E weather models showed the potential for a weak to locally 
moderate Santa Ana wind event, with gusty winds localized to mountain ridges in the 
backcountry areas. Wind-prone locations were projected to see isolated wind gusts over 
45 mph. The NWS was forecasting peak wind gusts of 45–50 mph, with relative humidity 
values dropping to 8–12%.  
Weather Conditions: Sixteen high temperature records were broken in the Southwestern 
California area during this event, and humidity levels dropped into the teens and single 
digits. The maximum wind gust recorded on SDG&E weather stations was 82 mph at Sill 
Hill, with six stations reaching or exceeding 60 mph, nine reaching or exceeding 56 mph, 
and 21 stations reaching or exceeding 45 mph. 19 SDG&E weather stations met or 
exceeded their 99th percentile wind gust, and 73 met or exceeded their 95th percentile 
wind gust. 
Local Fire Conditions and Fire Potential: Areas forecast to be the windiest still had 
patchy snow cover from the last storm, as well as damp and muddy soil conditions. This

created less of a fire concern, as it would take longer for the light flashy fuels to dry out 
than in the areas forecast to receive much lighter winds. With hot and dry weather 
conditions in place, the service territory was under a low-end Elevated FPI of 12. 
Local, State, and federal suppression resource levels were monitored and appeared to be 
adequately staffed throughout the weather event.  
Alternatives Considered  
In the days leading up to potential PSPS events, including the events described in this report, 
SDG&E meteorologists closely monitor weather forecasts to identify the specific areas most 
likely to experience weather conditions that warrant PSPS.  Operational groups use these 
targeted forecasts to strategically stage field crews and observers in areas anticipated to 
experience the most severe weather. 
Once fire weather conditions materialize, stations in SDG&E’s weather network provide 
reading of conditions including wind speeds, temperatures, and relative humidity every 30 
seconds.  This data is monitored in real time by staff at SDG&E’s EOC and used to 
determine if PSPS should be implemented.  This close monitoring and frequent updating of 
location-specific data enables SDG&E to implement PSPS only as a last resort when 
conditions warrant de-energization. 
After monitoring and considering weather conditions, de-energizations for public safety were 
not implemented during this event.  
Mitigation Measures to Decrease Utility-Caused Fire Risk in De-Energized Areas 
Not applicable as no areas were de-energized during this event.  
Conditions to Conclude the PSPS Event 
Similar to the decision to initiate PSPS protocols, the decision to conclude a PSPS event is 
based on a number of factors.  
During this event, SDG&E Meteorologists utilized real time weather station data and forecast 
models to determine critical fire weather conditions had peaked and were trending weaker, 
without any indication of potential resurgence of conditions that could necessitate PSPS. 
Based on favorable weather conditions and expiration of the Red Flag Warning, SDG&E’s 
UIC approved conclusion of the PSPS event and demobilization of SDG&E’s EOC.

2. All factors considered by SDG&E in its decision to de-energize, including wind speed, 
temperature,  humidity, and  vegetation  moisture  in  the  vicinity  of  the  de-energized 
circuits. 
Response:  
The decision to implement PSPS is not based on a single factor; numerous criteria are 
considered when making this decision.   
During the January 14–16 event, key bases for determining if PSPS were necessary included, 
but were not limited to: 
• The FPI was rated Elevated for all inland districts and Orange County on January 14 
and for all districts in SDG&E’s service area January 15–16; 
• Weather forecasts indicated the potential for Santa Ana winds with isolated gusts over 
45 mph, along with abnormally hot temperatures and very dry conditions;  
• The SAWTI was rated Moderate for January 14–16, indicating that upon ignition, fires 
will grow rapidly and will be difficult to control; 
• Official  NWS  
forecasts  mentioned

for  wind  gusts  of 45–50 mph,  with 
stronger localized gusts in the most wind-prone locations; 
• A Red Flag Warning was issued for portions of Orange County from January 14 at 
1600 through January 16 at 1600; 
• Wind climatology of each circuit or circuit segment to include the 95th and 99th 
percentile winds from nearly 10 years of collecting weather data every 10 minutes 
from every station.

Response: 
Starting on January 13, SDG&E notified customers in areas that would potentially be 
impacted by PSPS on January 14.  Notifications were made via outbound dialer, email, text 
message, and personal phone calls.  Helpful information was also shared on SDG&E’s 
websites (SDGE.com and SDGEnews.com), SDG&E Alerts app, SDG&E’s social media 
channels (Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Nextdoor) and with local, state, and national news 
media outlets.  
On January 13, SDG&E provided verbal notice of the potential PSPS event to the Office of 
the Governor of California and staff for Senator Toni Atkins. No additional communications 
to elected officials were made during this event, as conditions warranting implementation of 
PSPS did not materialize and no customers were de-energized.

11. A description and evaluation of engagement with local and state public safety partners and 
community partners in providing advanced outreach/notification during the PSPS event. 
Response:  
SDG&E works throughout the year leading up to wildfire season on education and outreach 
with its local and state public safety partners and community partners.  In 2020, education and 
outreach included in-person tours and trainings.  Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, SDG&E has 
conducted its education and outreach through virtual tours, webinars, and trainings. 
SDG&E worked extensively with state and regional partners throughout this event, including 
extensive and multiple daily briefings with representatives from CalOES, CPUC, CalOES 
Tribal Affairs, County OES and 2-1-1. Additionally, SDG&E partnered with San Diego 
County OES, AFN Working Group, 2-1-1 San Diego, 2-1-1 Orange County, and community-
based organizations (CBOs) to amplify key messaging through their databases and social 
media channels, and to translate PSPS notification into other languages.   
The following is a description of specific engagement during the January 14–16 event: 
Throughout the event, SDG&E remained engaged with its local and state public safety 
partners by providing advanced notification to all appropriate partners and monitoring its 
communication channels throughout the duration of the event.  
Immediately following the PSPS event, SDG&E distributed a one question online survey to 
public safety partners requesting they rate SDG&E’s level of engagement with their
